headline: 42 days out, Harris stumps for El-Sayed.
summary: Kamala Harris campaigned in Detroit on Tuesday with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Michigan's Senate seat, at a roundtable on Black maternal health. It was her first big stop of the midterms. She called the Senate a "stopgap on the abuses of this administration." A Suffolk poll has El-Sayed 7 points up on Republican Mike Rogers.

cover_question.q: Why does she want him to win?

cover_answer: He's on her team, and a Senate seat lasts six years.
table_question: Would you ask a famous friend to help you win, or go it alone?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Kamala Harris used to be the vice president. On Tuesday she went to Detroit to help a man named Abdul El-Sayed, who wants to be one of Michigan's two senators. It's like a famous player showing up at your game so more people come to watch. The voting is in November, and nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: A famous helper at a game is something they have seen. The Senate can wait.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script skips the Senate and keeps one picture: a famous player turning up at a game so more people come. That is what a campaign stop is, and it is enough. Expect "is she the boss?" Not any more. She used to be second in charge, and now she is helping a friend.

8-12.script: Michigan picks a senator on November 3, and the seat lasts six years. El-Sayed won a rough primary, and many voters on the losing side like Harris, so she came to bring them back, like a captain talking a teammate onto the field. She called the Senate a stopgap on the president: a brake.
8-12.why: A captain gathering a team, then a brake pedal.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out how groups hold together after a fight, and a primary is exactly that. The script hands them the chain: a rough primary, a split team, a famous captain sent to gather it, then a poll to check whether it worked. The brake is what Harris means by stopgap. Expect "is he going to win?" One poll says yes. Polls miss.

13-17.script: Harris said the Senate should be a "stopgap on the abuses of this administration." Is a senator's job to check the president, or to pass laws? Second: she lost Michigan in 2024. Does a candidate gain or lose by standing next to her?
13-17.why: Two questions with a real case for each side. Let them pick one.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a senator writes laws, and a senator can say no to a president. Harris is asking Michigan to hire one for the second job. Colder: why did El-Sayed's team want a candidate who lost the state? The script asks what they saw. Expect "is this just about Trump?" Partly. The seat outlasts him.

5-7.q: Why does she want him to win?
5-7.a: He's on her team. If he wins, he gets a vote in the Senate for six years.

8-12.a: A short-term fix. She means senators who vote no on the president.
One poll has him up 47 to 40. Polls miss, and the vote is November 3.

13-17.q: Why campaign with someone who lost the state?
13-17.a: Her voters backed his primary rival. He needs them, and she is still a big name.
Rogers's ad ties him to a streamer who said America deserved 9/11. El-Sayed has distanced himself. Judge his own words.
